extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics, playwrights, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for composing and judging classical dramatic genres (comedy, tragedy, epic) based on Aristotle's Art of Poetry with commentary. Covers subject-matter, emotional effects, structural parts, and temporal/spectral limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: principal object is ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy always proposes Ridicule for its Object; whatever is ridiculous may be the subject of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ridicule ought always to be the subject of Comedy; subjects should be those that are laughable rather than those that arouse pity, horror, or aversion. The commentator emphasizes that converting tragic subjects into ridicule (as Plautus does) makes them true comedies, but treating serious, painful crimes as mere spectacle conflicts with the aim of Comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: exclude subjects that cause pain, horror, or pity
rubrics_metrics.description: Banishes all that can cause Horror, Aversion, or Pity, as also what is too serious or severe from the Comick Theatre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic stage cannot make us laugh at things accompanied by real pain or destruction; therefore theft, adultery, murder and similar vices—when they provoke pity or horror—are excluded as proper subjects for Comedy. The commentator notes nuance: poets sometimes exposed notorious persons with 'a great deal of liberty' but presenting barefaced crimes as comedic subject-matter would oppose comedy's aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: permitted social status of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is not an imitation exclusively of low or deceitful people; it does not represent only the meanest persons and may bring eminent citizens and magistrates on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great persons can appear in comedy provided the treatment remains within ridiculing bounds; the majesty of princes is incompatible with comedy's nature, so 'heroic comedies' (serious high-style treatment of princes/heroes) are not appropriate. The expedient of labeling such works 'heroic comedies' is criticized as unnatural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: tonal register — light raillery vs biting invective
rubrics_metrics.description: New Comedy sought a graceful and slight touch — 'a cream of raillery and joke' — as opposed to the extravagant biting raillery of old Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedies that combine the light, pleasing ridicules (tickling the fancy) with occasional sharper satire (as Molière sometimes does) can be very successful; however, excessive malice or sustained invective conflicts with the comic aim once Laws and Customs moderated old Comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: structural/production elements (masks, prologue, actors, chorus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masks, prologues, and the augmentation of the number of actors were later additions to Comedy, likely borrowed from Tragedy; the Comick Chorus was officially allowed only late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle (as explained) calls everything before the first song of the Chorus a 'prologue' (exposition) whether it is a separate prologue or what later tradition calls a parabasis. Comedies may use masks and more actors, but these elements were adopted after Comedy had begun to take form; the Chorus was an institutional addition (magistrates gave the chorus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: function and placement of prologue/parabasis
rubrics_metrics.description: What Aristotle calls a Prologue is that which is before the first song of the Chorus and is so united to the subject that it cannot be separated; it may be an explanation of the subject or the parabasis where the poet addresses the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek drama did not have the separate modern prologue form; the explanatory material typically appears as part of the first scene (or as parabasis mid-play). Modern separate prologues (Terence, Plautus) are a later practice; when judging comic form, assess how exposition is integrated with the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: 'forming the subjects' — coherence of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'form the subjects' means to dispose and unite varied parts to make one coherent whole rather than a texture of gross railleries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old Comedy often consisted of disconnected invectives and rough raillery; the advance to 'forming the subjects' (Epicharmus, Phormys, Crates) meant organizing episodes into a coherent plot. When evaluating/composing comedy, prefer coherent subjects/plots over mere assortment of jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: definition — imitation of a serious, whole action of certain magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is Grave, Entire, and hath a Just Length; it must have a beginning, middle, and end and be of a determinate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper tragedy imitates an integrated action (not merely characters or manners), with an arc that produces cathartic effect through pity and terror. Assess whether the action is complete and proportionate in length; lacking beginning/middle/end renders the piece defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: six constituent parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must have six parts: (1) the Fable (plot), (2) Manners (characters), (3) Diction, (4) Sentiments (thought), (5) Decoration (spectacle), and (6) Music (melody).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the essential dimensions for composing or judging a tragedy. The commentator notes that some of these pertain to 'means' and others to 'matter'; plot is the most important, then characters, then thought/diction/music/spectacle in varying order of dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (Fable) is primary — action over character
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important is the Fable or the Composition of things: Tragedy is imitation not of Men but of their Actions; the subject (plot) is the principal and as it were the Soul of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating tragedy give priority to how well the action is constructed (unity, causal sequence, peripeties and recognitions). A work with weaker diction or decoration but a well-constituted plot will succeed more readily than one with fine diction but a poor subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters (Manners): their role and relative importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners (characters) are that which distinguishes the quality of those who act; they disclose inclinations and the part a person will take in events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy can subsist without detailed 'manners' but not without action; nevertheless, characters shape the plausibility of the plot. It is generally easier for poets to succeed in diction and manners than in forming a right subject (plot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Discourse) as verbal expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the explication of things by words; it is of equal force both in prose and verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clarity, appropriateness, rhetorical quality, and how diction conveys the action and thought. Diction interacts with music and verse to produce the tragic style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments / Thought (what is said and its cogency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments (thought) are the faculty of expressing those things which belong to the subject and are accessory to it; much of it pertains to rhetoric and common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the intellectual and argumentative content: plausibility of speeches, suitability of ideas to situation, and rhetorical composition. Ancient orators' styles differ; tragic thought should serve the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music / Melody as a central constituent
rubrics_metrics.description: Music (melody) is the most agreeable of all that Tragedy can possess and assists the imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although practices vary (verse-only vs verse+musical elements), melody and rhythm strongly affect the tragic impact. Consider how musical elements (chorus, sung parts) enhance emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration / Spectacle: external but impactful
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration is a part of Tragedy but does not properly regard the Art of the Poet; it is more the business of workmen and engineers and tragedy keeps force without representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle can augment the effect, but it is auxiliary to the poetic art. When judging, separate the poetic merits (plot, diction, thought) from the mere scenic embellishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and limits of time in Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ought to confine itself to the Circuit of the Sun (one day or one night) or as near as possible; actions should not be extended beyond reasonable temporal limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentator interprets Aristotle strictly: actions should be containable within the time of representation (Sophoclean models often only four hours). Small shifts in time are permissible when necessary, but allowing many hours/days undermines verisimilitude. Aristotle allows some flexibility (examples of up to eight or ten hours) but warns against excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic (Epopœia) vs Tragedy: medium and temporal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic is composed in verse, uses pure narration rather than dramatic representation, and has a larger extent; its time is indeterminate and may span years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic's means differ: narration permits long durations and varied styles; epic often imitates actions of great persons (by rank) rather than necessarily illustrious deeds. When assessing epic, judge its narrative design and suitable scope rather than applying dramatic Unity of Time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy effects — refinement (catharsis) of the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy, by means of compassion and terror, perfectly refines in us all sorts of passions and whatever is like them. 'To refine' here means to curb or regulate the excess of passions rather than to root them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's claim is a defense against Plato: the spectacle of properly ordered tragedy educates and moderates emotion. When composing/judging, consider whether pity and fear are elicited and then regulated rather than merely inflamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeties and recognitions as chief devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The most efficacious means which Tragedy uses to affect and please are the Peripeties and Recognizances; both are parts of the subject (plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the placement and plausibility of reversals and recognitions: they should emerge naturally from the plot and contribute to catharsis; their absence or mishandling weakens tragic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: On origin of comic/tragic subjects: true vs feigned
rubrics_metrics.description: Old (early) Comedy used 'true' subjects (not feigned adventures); feigned (invented) subjects arose later (new Comedy) and allowed dramatic invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical style or composing in an 'ancient' mode, note whether the work relies on true topical satire or constructed fictional adventures; both have conventions and implications for coherence and propriety.
